steps.title: Roman tradition
steps.body: Talhas are large clay pots, some holding over 1,000 litres, used in the Alentejo since Roman times. Wine was fermented and stored in them, especially around Vidigueira, Cuba and Vila de Frades. The tradition survived in family cellars, adegas, even as modern wineries took over.

steps.title: How it's made
steps.body: Crushed grapes, with skins and sometimes stems, ferment in the talha. The inside is coated with pez, a resin mixture, to seal it. Skins sink to the bottom and act as a natural filter. The wine stays on its skins until about St Martin's Day, November 11, when talhas are traditionally opened and the wine is drawn from a tap at the base.
steps.highlight: Fermented on skins, opened in November

steps.explanation: St Martin's Day marks the opening of the new talha wine.

steps.title: Recognition
steps.body: In 2010, the Alentejo DOC created the category DOC Alentejo Vinho de Talha for wines made this way, fermented and stored in clay until at least November 11. Whites, reds, orange wines and rosés can all be made. The style links to the global interest in amphora and skin-contact wines, like Georgia's qvevri.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Talhas are Roman clay pots still used in the Alentejo
Wine ferments on skins until St Martin's Day
DOC Vinho de Talha was created in 2010
